items.job: Open pull requests that move pinned dependency versions (SHA-pinned actions, lockfiles) in the GitHub-hosted repositories; advisory alerts are a hosted by-product.
items.reasons: Rule 1: jobs of the four: zizmor audits workflow security, actionlint checks workflow correctness, Syft inventories, attest signs provenance; none moves a pin. zizmor's docs hand hash-pin updates to Dependabot or Renovate, and zizmor audits dependabot.yml. Only overlap: zizmor known-vulnerable-actions with Dependabot alerts, Actions only. Rule 2: the job would otherwise have no owner, so documented capability decides; the hosted service is enabled by a checked-in .github/dependabot.yml and installs nothing on the host. Record B rejected only the self-hosted library path. A 2023 study with mixed findings (reduced technical lag) is supporting only. Maintained: HEAD 2026-10-01, v0.398.0 2026-09-28 (gh). Reading taken: 'pinned dependencies' includes keeping pins current; alerts and security updates are not the basis.

evidence.quote: Once your workflows and actions are hash-pinned, consider using [Dependabot] or [Renovate] to keep them up-to-date automatically.

Most people are familiar with the Dependabot service that runs on GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise. Enabling that is as simple as [checking a `dependabot.yml` configuration file in to your repository's `.github` directory]

When you enable Dependabot version updates for GitHub Actions, Dependabot will help ensure that references to actions in a repository's workflow.yml file and reusable workflows used inside workflows are kept up to date.
We obtain mixed findings. On the positive side, projects do reduce technical lag after Dependabot adoption and developers are highly receptive to its pull requests.

items.measurement: Enable .github/dependabot.yml (github-actions plus the repository's package ecosystems, 7-day cooldown) on one of this host's repositories for four weekly cycles, and Renovate (named by zizmor's docs, not a packet candidate) with equivalent rules on a fork. Metric: stale SHA pins and lockfile entries at start and end, update PRs merged with required checks green, PRs closed as wrong or noise. Overturn to do_not_install if no useful update merges; change owner if Renovate clears more stale pins with no more failed PRs.

items.job: Transport scanner SARIF into GitHub code scanning (upload-sarif); CodeQL semantic analysis, the repository's other function, is a separate job.
items.reasons: Rule 1: upload-sarif is transport, not a scanner. None of the four performs it, but its only consumer in the final set is zizmor, whose upstream integration already carries the step: zizmor-action pins and runs it (advanced-security default true) and the manual recipe prescribes it. It is a pinned dependency of zizmor's slot, not a separately owned job; actionlint annotates by default, Syft and attest emit no findings. The job belongs on public repositories; where code scanning is unavailable zizmor documents --format=github as the fallback and calls it more limited. CodeQL analysis itself is vulnerability tooling without the defined gap the layer packet requires. Maintained (4.38.2, 24 Sept 2026).

items.job: Open scheduled update pull requests that keep hash-pinned actions and manifest dependencies current, and raise advisory alerts and security-update pull requests for manifest dependencies.
items.reasons: Rule 1: none of the four opens update pull requests; zizmor and actionlint only detect unpinned or mismatched references, and zizmor's docs point hash-pinned users to Dependabot. The job belongs here: the requirement names pinned dependencies, and unmaintained pins go stale. Overlap: zizmor's known-vulnerable-actions checks actions against GitHub advisories, while Dependabot alerts skip SHA-pinned actions and cover manifests; zizmor's dependabot-cooldown and dependabot-execution audits lint dependabot.yml, not replace it. Rule 2: the job has no other owner, so documented capability decides; the owner is the hosted service enabled by a checked-in dependabot.yml, which installs nothing on the WSL2 host. Record A's objection applies to the dependabot-core library and CLI, which stay uninstalled. Gates pass: main commit 2026-10-01, release v0.398.0 2026-09-28.

Dependabot-Core is a library, so you'll need an entrypoint script of some kind.

items.item: CodeQL SARIF upload (github/codeql-action upload-sarif) as its own slot
items.job: Upload scanner SARIF output to GitHub code scanning so findings appear as alerts in the repository's security tab.

Rule 2: the requirement asks for scoped permissions and attributable hosted checks; a failing zizmor or actionlint step delivers that with nothing extra, while upstream states the upload mode needs security-events: write, does not fail on findings, and blocks only through a ruleset. I found no public measured gain. Gates pass (main commit 2026-09-29; code scanning is available on public repositories); that is eligibility, not a reason.

items.measurement: Target Windows 11 host on WSL 3.0.1 (per-distro cgroups isolated). Install both checksum-pinned images (26.04.1 48d56724..., 24.04.5 bb415d82...), run the identical bootstrap, record pass/fail per step: first boot to shell; `systemctl --user is-system-running`; `dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install`, `docker info` reporting cgroup v2 with the systemd driver, `docker run --memory 1g hello-world`; `nvidia-smi`; `docker run --rm --gpus all` on a CUDA image; `uv python install` and `uv run`; Node LTS install; `claude --version` and `codex --version` plus one headless prompt each. Overturned only if 26.04.1 fails a step that 24.04.5 passes and the documented in-release remedies (gnu-prefixed coreutils, `update-alternatives --set sudo /usr/bin/sudo.ws`) do not clear it.

items.item: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Canonical WSL image) as co-finalist or named fallback
items.job: The same job as item 1 (base distribution of the host); as a co-finalist or standby it would be a second owner of that job. Overlap: complete, with Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS.
items.reasons: Rule 1: the job has one owner; a co-finalist or standby image is a second owner of the same job, justified only by a documented 26.04 blocker on this host, and no fetched source shows one. Rule 3: it passes the same gates and no measurement favours it; it loses on seamlessness because standard support ends May 2029, two years earlier. Its cgroup v1 tolerance buys nothing here, since rootless Docker limits need cgroup v2. The 26.04 changes (uutils coreutils, sudo-rs) keep GNU coreutils and sudo.ws available in-release. The WSL 2.7.x shared-cgroup stop is a WSL property and no trigger for a fallback. It stays only as the comparison arm of the measurement.

evidence.quote: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Released: Apr 2024 | May 2029 | May 2034 | May 2034 | May 2039
cgroup is supported only when running with cgroup v2 and systemd.

In newer releases where the Rust-based implementations are the default, GNU Coreutils and sudo.ws remain available as providers, while the Rust-based implementations are the primary ones going forward.

All distro's systemd instances shared the same sets of cgroup. This will cause conflicts. For example, when booting multiple wsl distros at the same time. Only one can create the systemd user session successfully.

items.measurement: The same run as item 1. 24.04.5 returns (as the single default, never as a parallel install) only if 26.04.1 fails a step there that 24.04.5 passes under the identical bootstrap and WSL version, and the failure survives the documented in-release remedies. Metric: pass/fail per step. A failure that hits both images, or the WSL 2.7.x shared-cgroup stop, does not count.

Evidence weight: pass 1 cites Canonical's GPU how-to as a 26.04 deviceQuery PASS. The page says its commands target Ubuntu 26.04 AMD64, but its captured build log reads 'host compiler GNU 13.3.0' while the 26.04 release notes give GCC 15.2, so that log is not a 26.04 run. NVIDIA's CUDA 13.4 Linux guide lists Ubuntu 26.04.1 (kernel 7.0.0-31, GCC 15.2.0, glibc 2.43).

result.notes: The 2.7.13 first-boot stop matches a WSL defect: PR 40519 (released in 2.9.8, namespaces added in 2.9.13, stable in 3.0.1 on 2026-09-29) isolates per-distro cgroups; the 2.7.14 notes do not mention cgroup. Not verified on this host. On 26.04: `apt-key` is gone (skip NVIDIA's `apt-key del` step), the sudo-rs prompt differs, and `coreutils-from-gnu` may conflict with build-essential. rust-coreutils CVE fix status in 26.04.1 was not verified. Tools: ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_search, ctx_execute, gh (8 calls).

items.job: Base Linux distribution of the WSL2 developer host: systemd, userland and package base under rootless Docker, CUDA, uv, Node and both agents.
items.reasons: Rule 1: one job, base distribution; the only overlap is Ubuntu 24.04.5, so one owner. Rule 2: on a new host the job has no owner, so documented capability decides, and the WSL registry default `Ubuntu` already resolves to the 26.04.1 image. Rule 3: both releases pass every gate (amd64 WSL images dated 2026-08-27 and 2026-09-08, documented install, Claude Code needs Ubuntu 20.04+, Codex ships a musl Linux x86_64 binary). No public measurement found that separates them. Seamlessness decides: registry default, Canonical's current WSL release, support to April 2031 against May 2029, and Docker Engine, NVIDIA Container Toolkit and CUDA all list 26.04. Its cgroup-v2-only systemd matches rootless Docker's requirement; uv supplies Python, so the 3.14 default is neutral.

items.job: The same job, base Linux distribution of the WSL2 host; as a named fallback it owns no job until a rollback is triggered.
items.reasons: Rule 1: it competes for the same single job, so it cannot stay a co-finalist. Rule 2: a second image is an extra install and no public measurement shows a gain. Rule 3: it passes the same gates but loses on seamlessness: not the registry default, and standard support ends 31 May 2029. The 26.04 changes that can break scripts have documented in-place remedies (GNU coreutils via coreutils-from-gnu, classic sudo as sudo.ws), and Docker's and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit's install commands use keyring files, so the removed apt-key does not block them. Fallback: keep 24.04.5 only as a named rollback target, never installed or bootstrapped ahead of a trigger; its checksum-pinned image stays one registry command away.

result.notes: 26.04 points to plan for: release notes list 20 rust-coreutils CVEs and an ACL `mkdir -p` bug (remedy: coreutils-from-gnu); sudo-rs (remedy: sudo.ws); apt-key is removed, so skip the `apt-key del` step in NVIDIA's WSL guide; /tmp is tmpfs. Install as `Ubuntu-26.04` or the checksum-verified file, because `Ubuntu` follows the newest LTS. 24.04.5: named rollback only, not installed. NVIDIA Container Toolkit lists both releases. Per-distribution cgroups belong to the WSL layer (2.9.8 #40519, 2.9.13 #41512). gh calls used: 4.
